lead: The ears locate a sound from small differences between the two eardrums: arrival time, loudness and the filtering of the pinna. A 3D sound display exists because a visual scene without direction-aware audio feels flat, and because audio can point to events outside the screen. It is used in VR headsets, AR navigation, flight simulators, games and telepresence. The display must control the cues at each ear, not just play stereo. This chapter covers the ear, the three localisation cues and the main sound display types.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.1 for the output channel view; no earlier acoustics is assumed.

sections.h3: The ear as a frequency analyser

blocks.text: Sound is a pressure wave in air. The outer ear, or pinna, collects it; the ear canal guides it to the eardrum, a thin membrane. Three small bones, the ossicles, pass the vibration to the cochlea. The cochlea is a coiled, fluid-filled tube. Along its basilar membrane, high frequencies peak near the base and low frequencies near the apex. Hair cells turn that motion into nerve pulses on the auditory nerve. This place code makes the cochlea a frequency analyser. A healthy young ear hears about 20 Hz to 20 kHz; one hertz is one cycle per second. The upper limit falls with age and noise damage. The pinna is not a simple funnel: its ridges create small reflections and notches that depend on direction. That is why the shape of your own ear matters.
Direction comes from three cues. The first is interaural time difference (ITD), the arrival-time gap between ears.

blocks.where: ITD is the interaural time difference in seconds; d is the ear spacing, about 0.175 m; θ is the angle from straight ahead in degrees; c is the speed of sound, about 343 m/s.

blocks.text: Using d = 0.175 m and c = 343 m/s, the straight-line formula gives a maximum of about 0.5 ms at θ = 90°. The commonly quoted maximum is about 0.6–0.7 ms; it is larger because sound also travels around the curved surface of the head, which the straight-line formula ignores. ITD is useful below about 1.5 kHz because low-frequency waves have long wavelengths and the phase difference between ears is unambiguous. Above that, phase wraps.

The second cue is interaural level difference (ILD). The head blocks short wavelengths, so the near ear receives more high-frequency energy. ILD is a few dB to about 20 dB and is useful above about 1.5 kHz. The third cue is the direction-dependent filtering of the pinna, head and torso. It is captured by the head-related transfer function (HRTF): the ratio of the pressure at an eardrum to the pressure in the free field for a given direction and frequency. HRTF supplies spectral notches that help with elevation and front-back.

Front-back confusion happens because a front and a rear source can give similar ITD and ILD; the set of such directions is a cone of confusion. Small head movements break the tie: the brain compares the change in cues with the known movement. A static binaural render therefore feels less external than a head-tracked one.
Sound displays differ in how many ears they control.

items: One loudspeaker gives no direction. It is enough for alarms and speech.
A stereo pair uses two loudspeakers. Panning sets a phantom source between them by level and delay. It works only near the sweet spot and mainly in the horizontal plane.
A multi-speaker surround system places speakers around the listener. It adds directions but still depends on room and listener position.

Wave field synthesis uses a line of many closely spaced loudspeakers. Each speaker gets a delay and gain so their wavefronts add to the wavefront of a virtual source. One line creates a convincing front stage, not full 3D around the room.

Headphones with binaural rendering feed each ear a signal filtered by an HRTF. This is the usual VR choice. A stereo loudspeaker pair can also deliver binaural audio, but the left loudspeaker reaches both ears. Cross-talk cancellation filters each channel so the left speaker cancels at the right ear and vice versa. It needs a fixed or tracked listener.

blocks.text: Head tracking updates the HRTF as the head turns. This gives dynamic cues, reduces front-back errors and keeps the scene fixed in space. Audio-visual sync tolerates tens of milliseconds, more for audio lagging video than for audio leading it: audio that leads the picture is noticed beyond roughly 45 ms, while audio lagging the picture is tolerated up to roughly 125 ms. Interactive audio needs low latency; a common target is under about 20–40 ms.

figure.caption: A click 30° right, with ear spacing 0.175 m, has an extra path of 0.0875 m. The right ear receives it first; the left ear is delayed by 0.255 ms, or 11 samples at 44.1 kHz.

spec.title: Worked example: click 30° right
spec.aria: A click 30 degrees to the right with ear spacing 0.175 metres gives an extra path of 0.0875 metres and reaches the right ear first, while the left ear is delayed by 0.255 milliseconds or 11 samples at 44.1 kilohertz; headphones replay both ear signals and the listener perceives the direction.

examples.question: A click comes from 30 degrees to the right of straight ahead. The ears are 17.5 cm apart and the speed of sound is 343 m/s. Find the interaural time difference and the delay in samples at 44.1 kHz.
steps: Ear spacing d = 0.175 m; angle θ = 30°; speed c = 343 m/s; sample rate f_s = 44100 Hz.
Extra path length = d × sin θ = 0.175 × sin 30° = 0.175 × 0.5 = 0.0875 m.
Delay in samples = ITD × f_s = 2.55102 × 10⁻⁴ × 44100 = 11.25 samples, rounded to 11 samples.
examples.answer: The extra path is 0.0875 m, the ITD is 2.55102 × 10⁻⁴ s (0.255102 ms), and the far-ear delay is 11.25 samples, rounded to 11 samples at 44.1 kHz.
examples.check:
import math
d = 0.175
theta_deg = 30.0
c = 343.0
fs = 44100.0
theta = math.radians(theta_deg)
extra = d * math.sin(theta)
itd = extra / c
itd_ms = itd * 1000.0
n = itd * fs
print(f"{extra:.6f}")
print(f"{itd:.9f}")
print(f"{itd_ms:.6f}")
print(f"{n:.6f}")

traps: Using ITD for all frequencies. Above about 1.5 kHz the phase difference is ambiguous, and the brain uses level difference and pinna filtering instead.
Forgetting front-back confusion. A front and a rear source can share ITD and ILD; the pinna and small head movements resolve the tie.
Delaying the wrong ear. Sound arrives first at the near ear, so the far ear is delayed. A right-side source means the left ear is delayed.
Treating HRTF as ordinary headphone equalisation. An HRTF is direction and frequency dependent; a fixed equaliser is not.
Calling stereo panning full 3D audio. Plain stereo has no elevation and weak front-back cues without HRTF and head tracking.

quiz.q: State the typical hearing range of a healthy young human ear and define the hertz.
quiz.a: About 20 Hz to 20 kHz. One hertz is one cycle per second.

quiz.q: Why is interaural time difference useful mainly below about 1.5 kHz?
quiz.a: At low frequencies the wavelength is long compared with the ear spacing, so the phase difference between the two ears is unambiguous. Above about 1.5 kHz the phase difference wraps, so the brain relies more on level difference and pinna filtering.

quiz.q: A source is 60° to the right. Ear spacing is 0.175 m, speed of sound is 343 m/s, sample rate is 48 kHz. Find the extra path, the ITD in ms and the delay in samples.
Explain front-back confusion and two ways a listener resolves it.
quiz.a: A source in front and a source behind can produce similar ITD and ILD, so they lie on a cone of confusion. The pinna adds direction-dependent spectral notches that differ front and back. Small head movements also change the cues in a way the brain can compare with the known movement.

quiz.q: Define HRTF and say why it depends on direction and frequency.
quiz.a: The head-related transfer function is the ratio of the pressure at an eardrum to the free-field pressure for a given direction and frequency. The pinna, head and torso scatter and reflect sound differently at different angles and wavelengths, so the filter changes with both.

quiz.q: Why does a two-loudspeaker binaural system need cross-talk cancellation?
quiz.a: Each loudspeaker reaches both ears. Without cancellation, the left channel leaks into the right ear and the right channel into the left ear, which blurs the intended ITD and ILD. Cross-talk cancellation filters each channel so the left speaker cancels at the right ear and vice versa. It works best for a fixed or tracked listener.

quiz.q: An XR demo has audio lagging video by 80 ms. Is this within the usual lip-sync tolerance?
quiz.a: For broadcast-style lip sync, 80 ms of audio lag is inside the usual tolerance and is mostly not noticed. In interactive XR, where sound must follow a head turn or a touch, 80 ms is at the edge and should be reduced to roughly 20–40 ms.

quiz.q: Name the three main localisation cues used by the human auditory system.
quiz.a: Interaural time difference, interaural level difference and pinna/head-related filtering, captured by the HRTF.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, game engines and XR toolkits use HRTF plugins, ambisonics and head-tracked binaural audio. Research personalises HRTFs from photos or ear scans and uses wave field synthesis for large rooms. Search terms: ambisonics, HRTF personalisation, cross-talk cancellation, wave field synthesis, MPEG-H audio.
